1 · Intro

When to use it.

Non-exempt pay is built from hours and pay rules. When a rule is misread or a time card is coded wrong, the paycheck is wrong even though every punch is there.

This draft covers the federal rules, which set the floor. Vanderbilt's own rules for holidays, shift differentials, and on-call pay are being documented by Payroll and are listed as open items.

Use this whenA manager or employee asks how overtime, a holiday, a shift, or on-call time is paid, or a time card total looks wrong.

2 · Walk through

The rules that change pay.

Check off each item as you read.

Watch-outs

  • These are the federal rules. A state where the employee works can require more.
  • Never remove or reduce hours an employee worked to avoid overtime.
  • Open item: Vanderbilt's rule on whether paid time off and holidays count toward overtime, and which seven days make the overtime workweek. The published calendar shows weekly pay periods running Monday to Sunday and biweekly periods Sunday to Saturday.
  • Open item: Vanderbilt's holiday pay rules, shift differential rates, on-call and call-back pay, and the UKG pay code for each. Payroll is documenting these.

Official documentation

Vendor documentation describes the standard process. Vanderbilt's setup, codes, and rules in this course take priority.

3 · Knowledge check

Check your understanding.

Three questions. You get feedback on each answer. All three right completes the course.

Q1A biweekly employee works 30 hours in week one and 50 in week two. How many overtime hours?

Q2An employee stayed late without approval and worked 3 extra hours. What happens to those hours?

Q3A manager asks whether working a holiday is automatically overtime. What do you say?

HCM Academy job aid · Payroll & Timecards

Pay rules: overtime, holidays, shifts, and on-call

Use when: A manager or employee asks how overtime, a holiday, a shift, or on-call time is paid, or a time card total looks wrong. · System: Overview

  1. Start with who the rules apply to.
  2. Overtime: more than 40 hours worked in a workweek.
    • Over 40 hours worked in the workweek: overtime.
    • Weekend or holiday work by itself: not overtime under federal law.
  3. Count each workweek on its own.
  4. Count hours worked, not hours paid.
  5. Holidays: paid by policy, not by federal law.
  6. Shift differentials: paid by policy, and they raise the overtime rate.
  7. On-call time: it depends on how free the employee is.
    • Required to stay at the work site: hours worked.
    • At home and free to use the time: generally not hours worked.
    • Called in to work: the time spent working counts.
  8. Unapproved overtime still gets paid.
  9. Check the time card, then ask payroll.

Watch-outs

  • These are the federal rules. A state where the employee works can require more.
  • Never remove or reduce hours an employee worked to avoid overtime.
  • Open item: Vanderbilt's rule on whether paid time off and holidays count toward overtime, and which seven days make the overtime workweek. The published calendar shows weekly pay periods running Monday to Sunday and biweekly periods Sunday to Saturday.
  • Open item: Vanderbilt's holiday pay rules, shift differential rates, on-call and call-back pay, and the UKG pay code for each. Payroll is documenting these.
